pass_a_gloss: [...] and hard to face was Israel, for this reason indeed very bitterly and with love of mischief, removing from him his help, they persuaded him to offend the God over all. And they continued to the end having such a mind, and if it happened that Israel, having offended God, shared in misfortunes, those boasted over and jeered, accusing God of being able to do nothing at all, he who promises to save those who worship him. And of this a witness is the blessed Jeremiah in the vision against them, saying: The horn of Moab was broken, and his arm was shattered. Make him drunk, because he was magnified against the Lord. And again: For thus said the Lord, Arioth was taken, and strongholds were seized. And Moab will perish from being a people, because he was magnified against the Lord. For at times the tyrant of the Assyrians and Babylonians came to ravage Judaea. And he took the cities of Samaria. And the Moabites again, smiling down on those who had perished, mocked not moderately, and continued reproaching the glory of God. For this reason they too have been given to desolation, and have perished utterly, together with cities and people and every house, so that already somehow they seem not even to have existed. The vision set before us, then, remembers the things that befell them, from wrath clearly from above, and says: [Lemma, Isaiah 15:1:] By night the Moabite will perish; for by night the wall of the land of Moab will perish. Some of those who have examined these things exactly have handed down that, when the Babylonians were about to raise war against them, an earthquake having happened, the mother city of the Moabites was shaken so much that its whole wall was shaken down of itself in night and darkness; and this having happened, before the attack of the enemies, all but perished for them the hope of safety. For this reason he says that the land of Moab will perish by night. [Lemma, Isaiah 15:2:] But grieve, he says, over yourselves. Similar as if he should say: Very many times, lifting a high brow, you revelled in the misfortunes of others; but now the war runs against you yourselves, and the harms from it hang over your unholy heads. Grieve then not over some others, but over yourselves. [Lemma:] For Lebedon will perish, where your altar is. I said that the Moabites had become fierce and haughty, both trusting in the deceits of the demons and thinking through the magic art to prevail over the hand of all, and of Israel himself, even if God should defend; so in the place called Lebedon there was for them an altar and precinct not unworthy of wonder, as far as concerns its construction. There they performed the divinations, and thought much of themselves, and made the place most revered beside the others. But there will perish, he says, also the workshop of your divination. [Lemma:] There you will go up [the section breaks off].
pass_b_english: …Israel was formidable and hard to face. So, with great bitterness and a love of mischief, they set about stripping him of his help and persuaded him to offend the God who is over all.

They kept this attitude to the very end. Whenever Israel had offended God and happened to fall into misfortune, they boasted over him and jeered, charging God with being utterly powerless, the God who promises to save those who worship him.

The blessed Jeremiah is witness to this in his vision against them, where he says: “The horn of Moab is broken, and his arm is shattered. Make him drunk, for he magnified himself against the Lord” (Jeremiah 48:25–26). And again: “For thus says the Lord: Arioth is taken, and the strongholds are seized. And Moab will perish as a people, for he magnified himself against the Lord” (Jeremiah 48:40–42).

For in time the tyrant of the Assyrians and Babylonians came to lay Judea waste, and he took the cities of Samaria. The Moabites, for their part, smiled at those who had perished, mocked them beyond measure, and went on heaping insult on the glory of God.
For this reason they too have been given over to desolation and have utterly perished, cities, people, and every household together, so that now it seems almost as if they had never existed.
The vision before us, then, recalls what befell them, plainly by wrath from above, and says: “By night the Moabite will perish; for by night the wall of the land of Moab will perish” (Isaiah 15:1).

Some who have studied these matters closely have handed down that, when the Babylonians were about to make war on them, an earthquake struck and shook the chief city of the Moabites so violently that its whole wall fell of itself in the night and the dark. When this happened, before the enemy attacked, their hope of safety all but perished. That is why he says that the land of Moab will perish by night.

“But grieve,” he says, “over yourselves” (Isaiah 15:2). It is as if he said: Many times you raised your brows high and gloated over the misfortunes of others; but now the war is running against you yourselves, and the harm that comes of it hangs over your unholy heads. Grieve, then, not over any others, but over yourselves.

“For Lebedon will perish, where your altar is” (Isaiah 15:2). I said that the Moabites had become fierce and arrogant, trusting in the deceits of demons and supposing that by the magician's art they would prevail over the power of all, even of Israel himself, though God should defend him. So in the place called Lebedon they had an altar and a sacred precinct of no ordinary construction. There they performed their divinations and prided themselves greatly, and they held the place more sacred than any other. But, he says, even the workshop of your divination will perish.

choices.why: The Moabites remove Israel's help from God by luring him into sin; they are not withdrawing their own support.

choices.english: charging God with being utterly powerless
choices.why: κατηγορέω with the genitive of the person: they accuse God of being able to do nothing.
rejected: saying that they could do nothing

choices.english: the tyrant of the Assyrians and Babylonians
choices.why: 70.400 is the Patrologia column number, not a figure in the text; the sentence is about the tyrant.
ἐντρυφάω with the dative of others' misfortunes is to revel in them.
Cyril's scornful word for the shrine is kept.
